content_blocks.text: Challenges under the Procurement Act
FAQs

Note that market engagement is now explicitly covered in the Procurement Act, would market engagement activity now be more directly subject to challenge? And if so, what factors do you envisage may be relevant?
heading_path: Note that market engagement is now explicitly covered in the Procurement Act, would market engagement activity now be more directly subject to challenge? And if so, what factors do you envisage may be relevant?

content_blocks.text: The requirements to treat bidders equally and transparently is already there in the Public Contracts Regulations 2015 ( PCR ) and this continues via section 16 of the Act.
heading_path: Note that market engagement is now explicitly covered in the Procurement Act, would market engagement activity now be more directly subject to challenge? And if so, what factors do you envisage may be relevant?

content_blocks.text: The difference under the Act is the new obligation at section 17 is to publish a Preliminary Market Engagement Notice ( PME Notice ) whenever the authority carries out preliminary market engagement (unless there are compelling reasons not to do so).
heading_path: Note that market engagement is now explicitly covered in the Procurement Act, would market engagement activity now be more directly subject to challenge? And if so, what factors do you envisage may be relevant?

content_blocks.text: Whether this will lead to increased challenges (presumably on the basis that the preliminary market engagement has given a competitor an unfair advantage?) will presumably depend on the content requirements of the PME Notice.
heading_path: Note that market engagement is now explicitly covered in the Procurement Act, would market engagement activity now be more directly subject to challenge? And if so, what factors do you envisage may be relevant?

content_blocks.text: The PME Notice will need to set out the requirements listed in regulation 17 of the Procurement Regulations 2024, which is essentially “ a description of the process by which the contracting authority proposes to engage, or has engaged, with suppliers during the preliminary market engagement. ”
heading_path: Note that market engagement is now explicitly covered in the Procurement Act, would market engagement activity now be more directly subject to challenge? And if so, what factors do you envisage may be relevant?

content_blocks.text: The official guidance on preliminary market engagement suggests that “ the notice can be used to share engagement outputs and ensure a wider audience is kept informed about the contracting authority's emerging thinking, therefore supporting the objectives of section 12 and ensuring all suppliers have access to the same information. The notice can also flag additional upcoming engagement opportunities .”
heading_path: Note that market engagement is now explicitly covered in the Procurement Act, would market engagement activity now be more directly subject to challenge? And if so, what factors do you envisage may be relevant?

content_blocks.text: There does not appear to be anything in these requirements that means that the authority must for example, provide in the (public) PME Notice a list of every supplier it has engaged with, discussions had and outcomes arrived at (although of course it may be necessary to share this information with candidates/tenderers in a procurement in order to meet the duties at section 16 and the guidance certainly seems to point to it being best practice to give significant narrative detail in the PME Notice).
heading_path: Note that market engagement is now explicitly covered in the Procurement Act, would market engagement activity now be more directly subject to challenge? And if so, what factors do you envisage may be relevant?

content_blocks.text: It certainly seems possible that increased transparency around PME Notices might lead to increased challenges – it will depend on the level of detail disclosed. It is of course always the case that, in order to bring a challenge, a supplier needs to show not only that there has been a breach, but that this has caused it to suffer or risk suffering a loss. Query if this might be difficult for a supplier to substantiate in relation to an alleged breach at PME stage.
heading_path: Note that market engagement is now explicitly covered in the Procurement Act, would market engagement activity now be more directly subject to challenge? And if so, what factors do you envisage may be relevant?

content_blocks.text: You mention, that for contracts valued over £5m, unsuccessful supplier names will be published in the Contract Award notice as well as successful supplier names. Is this related to the works threshold - or for goods and services too?
heading_path: You mention, that for contracts valued over £5m, unsuccessful supplier names will be published in the Contract Award notice as well as successful supplier names. Is this related to the works threshold - or for goods and services too?

content_blocks.text: No, this is not related to any of the goods/services/works thresholds – it is a separate standalone requirement in relation to any “public contract” valued at over £5m. Note that a works threshold which is valued at over £5m but still under the works threshold (£5,372,609) is not a “public contract” – and therefore it is not subject to this requirement.
heading_path: You mention, that for contracts valued over £5m, unsuccessful supplier names will be published in the Contract Award notice as well as successful supplier names. Is this related to the works threshold - or for goods and services too?

content_blocks.text: Can the new standstill period be paused, extended, or restarted to deal with potential supplier challenges?
heading_path: Can the new standstill period be paused, extended, or restarted to deal with potential supplier challenges?

content_blocks.text: Yes, there is nothing in the Act to say otherwise. Given that the mechanism for commencing (and therefore determining the end date of) the standstill period is the publication of the new Contract Award Notice, it seems likely that a new Contract Award Notice would need to be published (or the original notice updated).
heading_path: Can the new standstill period be paused, extended, or restarted to deal with potential supplier challenges?

content_blocks.text: If a standstill period is extended e.g. due to a threatened challenge, will automatic suspension still be available throughout that extended period?
heading_path: If a standstill period is extended e.g. due to a threatened challenge, will automatic suspension still be available throughout that extended period?

content_blocks.text: On our reading, yes, it will still be available. Section 101(1) is the operative provision on automatic suspensions, and this refers to “ any applicable standstill period ”. In our view this would extend to cover extensions to the standstill period.
heading_path: If a standstill period is extended e.g. due to a threatened challenge, will automatic suspension still be available throughout that extended period?

content_blocks.text: Does publication of the Contract Award Notice constitute day one or day zero of the standstill period?
heading_path: Does publication of the Contract Award Notice constitute day one or day zero of the standstill period?

content_blocks.text: Section 51(2) says that the standstill period is “ a period of eight working days beginning with the day on which a contract award notice is published ”. The publication date of the CAN is therefore day one.
heading_path: Does publication of the Contract Award Notice constitute day one or day zero of the standstill period?

content_blocks.text: Will it still be the case that award letters do not need to be sent to suppliers where the contracting authority awards a contract under a framework agreement or a dynamic purchasing system?
heading_path: Will it still be the case that award letters do not need to be sent to suppliers where the contracting authority awards a contract under a framework agreement or a dynamic purchasing system?

content_blocks.text: No; this is changing.
heading_path: Will it still be the case that award letters do not need to be sent to suppliers where the contracting authority awards a contract under a framework agreement or a dynamic purchasing system?

content_blocks.text: Under the Act, section 50 makes it mandatory to publish a Contract Award Notice (which itself contains a requirement to state that an award letter/assessment summary has been sent to tenderers) in relation to all “public contracts”. “Public contract” is defined at section 3(2) and includes call-off contracts from frameworks and DPS where these are over the relevant threshold.
heading_path: Will it still be the case that award letters do not need to be sent to suppliers where the contracting authority awards a contract under a framework agreement or a dynamic purchasing system?

content_blocks.text: With regards to the new standstill period being 8 working days, does this relate to the days which are worked at the individual institution (considering bank holidays or shutdowns etc), general working days in England or something else? Public holidays are different around the world & how would we know whether a working day for us is a working day in another country if returns are received from overseas suppliers?
heading_path: With regards to the new standstill period being 8 working days, does this relate to the days which are worked at the individual institution (considering bank holidays or shutdowns etc), general working days in England or something else? Public holidays are different around the world & how would we know whether a working day for us is a working day in another country if returns are received from overseas suppliers?

content_blocks.text: “Working day” has a precise meaning under the Act. It means any day which is not (a) a Saturday or a Sunday, or (b) a day which is a bank holiday in any part of the United Kingdom under the Banking and Financial Dealings Act 1971.

content_blocks.text: I presume the new notice requirements will apply to 'above threshold' procurements. Can you tell us please what the notice requirements will be for below threshold tenders?
heading_path: I presume the new notice requirements will apply to 'above threshold' procurements. Can you tell us please what the notice requirements will be for below threshold tenders?

content_blocks.text: Yes, in general the notice requirements apply to “public contracts”. An under-threshold contract will not be a “public contract”. However, part 6 of the Act deals with below threshold contracts. If a contract is under threshold but over £12,000 (central government authorities) or £30,000 (all other contracting authorities) then it will be a “notifiable below threshold contract”.
heading_path: I presume the new notice requirements will apply to 'above threshold' procurements. Can you tell us please what the notice requirements will be for below threshold tenders?

content_blocks.text: This means that: (a) if the authority chooses to advertise the opportunity, it must publish a Below Threshold Tender Notice; and (b) as soon as reasonably practicable after awarding the contract, it must publish a Below Threshold Contract Details Notice. These requirements mirror the current Contracts Finder requirements under the PCR.
heading_path: I presume the new notice requirements will apply to 'above threshold' procurements. Can you tell us please what the notice requirements will be for below threshold tenders?

heading_path: I'm unsure what contracts the discussed changes apply to. Some are obvious and talk about a £5m threshold. What about lower value contracts - when do the additional notice periods and levels of transparency apply?

content_blocks.text: The new notices and transparency regime applies to all “public contracts”. This includes all contracts, framework agreements, and call-off contracts whose value is over the relevant value thresholds. You can find these thresholds here .
heading_path: I'm unsure what contracts the discussed changes apply to. Some are obvious and talk about a £5m threshold. What about lower value contracts - when do the additional notice periods and levels of transparency apply?

content_blocks.text: As discussed in the question immediately above, a couple of the notice requirements also apply where the contract value is below these thresholds but above £12,000 (central government authorities) or £30,000 (all other contracting authorities).
